subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the derivative of tan⁻¹(sec x + tan x).

mark_split.label: Combine the bracket over cos x
Write both parts in half angles

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what sec x + tan x simplifies to before you differentiate.

steps.label: Combine the bracket over cos x
steps.margin_note: First mark. Simplifying before differentiating is the method being tested. Differentiating the bracket as it stands also works and cancels to 1/2, but it takes more lines.
lines: Let y = Tan⁻¹(sec x + tan x)
sec x + tan x = 1/cos x + sin x/cos x = (1 + sin x) / cos x

recall.must_convey: That sec x + tan x is first written as the single fraction (1 + sin x)/cos x.
accept: write sec x plus tan x as one plus sin x over cos x
simplify the bracket before differentiating
both terms have cos x in the denominator so combine them
sec x plus tan x ni one plus sin x by cos x ga rayali
take cos x common in the denominator

steps.why: Differentiating the bracket as it stands puts the derivative of sec x + tan x over 1 + (sec x + tan x)², and that has to be factorised before it cancels. One line of algebra removes all of that work.
common_mistakes: Differentiating Tan⁻¹(sec x + tan x) directly with the chain rule and stopping at an unsimplified expression.
Writing sec x as cos x rather than 1/cos x.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever an inverse trigonometric function has a bracket, simplify the bracket first and differentiate last.

steps.label: Write both parts in half angles
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 1 + sin x is a perfect square in the half angles, and cos x factorises with the same bracket — that shared factor is what cancels.
lines: 1 + sin x = cos²(x/2) + sin²(x/2) + 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2) = (cos(x/2) + sin(x/2))²
cos x = cos²(x/2) − sin²(x/2) = (cos(x/2) + sin(x/2))(cos(x/2) − sin(x/2))

recall.must_convey: That 1 + sin x = (cos(x/2) + sin(x/2))², cos x factorises with the same bracket, and one factor cancels.
accept: one plus sin x is cos half x plus sin half x whole squared
cos x factorises into the sum and the difference of the half angles
the common bracket cancels leaving sum over difference
one plus sin x perfect square avuthundi half angles lo
use sin squared plus cos squared equals one to build the square

steps.why: Writing 1 as sin²(x/2) + cos²(x/2) turns 1 + sin x into a perfect square, and cos x carries the same bracket as a factor, so the fraction shortens by one cancellation.
common_mistakes: Writing cos x as cos²(x/2) + sin²(x/2), which equals 1, instead of the difference.
Forgetting the middle term 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2) when expanding the square.
steps.memory_tip: sin x = 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2) is the middle term of the square, so 1 + sin x is always a perfect square.

steps.label: Recognise tan(π/4 + x/2)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. This is the identity the question is built on. For −π/2 < x < π/2 the angle π/4 + x/2 lies in (0, π/2), inside the principal range, so the inverse tangent cancels the tangent exactly.
lines: Divide numerator and denominator by cos(x/2):
= (1 + tan(x/2)) / (1 − tan(x/2)) = tan(π/4 + x/2),  since tan(π/4) = 1
For −π/2 < x < π/2, the angle π/4 + x/2 lies in (0, π/2), so

recall.must_convey: That the fraction is tan(π/4 + x/2), so y = π/4 + x/2 on the stated interval.
accept: one plus tan half x over one minus tan half x is tan of pi by four plus x by two
the whole bracket is the tangent of pi by four plus half x
y becomes pi by four plus x by two
tan of pi by four plus x by two vasthundi
the inverse tangent cancels the tangent inside the principal range

steps.why: tan(A + B) with A = π/4 gives exactly (1 + tan B)/(1 − tan B), so the whole bracket is a single tangent and the inverse tangent removes it.
common_mistakes: Reading (1 + tan(x/2))/(1 − tan(x/2)) as tan(π/4) + tan(x/2).
Cancelling the inverse tangent without checking the angle lies in the principal range.
steps.memory_tip: tan(π/4) = 1, so any fraction of the form (1 + tan B)/(1 − tan B) is tan(π/4 + B).

steps.label: Differentiate the simple form
steps.margin_note: Last mark. π/4 is a constant and differentiates to 0, so the whole derivative comes from x/2.
lines: y = π/4 + x/2, and π/4 is a constant

accept: pi by four is a constant so the derivative is one half
the answer is one by two
only x by two differentiates and it gives half
pi by four constant kabatti derivative one by two
the derivative is a constant one half

steps.why: After the simplification the function is a straight line in x, so its derivative is the constant slope 1/2 — no trigonometric term survives.
common_mistakes: Differentiating π/4 as π/4 rather than 0.
Giving 2 instead of 1/2 by differentiating x/2 as 2x.
steps.memory_tip: Check with two values inside the range: y(0) = π/4 and y(π/3) = π/4 + π/6, and the rise π/6 over the run π/3 is 1/2.

insider_note: Write sec x + tan x as (1 + sin x)/cos x, then use half angles on both — the common factor cancels and leaves tan(π/4 + x/2). The answer is the constant ½.
